title: Trace a shadow with chalk three times a day
description: Draw around a friend's shadow in the morning, at noon and in the afternoon, and the pavement itself will show you how the Sun's path bends the day.

body.heading: Morning outline
paragraphs: Stand your partner on flat pavement in morning sunshine and chalk carefully around their shadow, head to feet. Write the time beside the head. The shadow will be long — much longer than the person who cast it.
Choose a shadow-caster who can stand still for a minute: a fence post or a chair works if nobody wants to pose, and a fixed object makes the three drawings easier to compare.

body.heading: Noon and afternoon
paragraphs: Return at midday and trace again from exactly the same spot. The shadow has shrunk and swung around. By afternoon it stretches out again, pointing the other way — three chalk people lying at three angles, all cast by one Sun moving across one sky.
Photograph the pavement before the rain or the street sweeper edits your work. The three outlines together are a sundial drawn by the day itself.

takeaway: Chalk the same shadow in the morning, at noon and in the afternoon: long, short, long again — the pavement becomes a sundial drawn by the day itself.
materials: A flat, sunny patch of pavement
A clock or phone to note the times
supervision: An adult should choose a pavement away from traffic and stay nearby while children work near any road.
safetyNotes: Work only on pavements and driveways, never in the road itself.
Wear a hat and sunscreen for the midday tracing.
Ask before chalking on anyone else's property.
